key_terms.meaning: A program in execution, with its own code, data, stack, registers and program counter; it is the unit of work the OS schedules.
The OS record for one process: process id, state, program counter, saved CPU registers, memory limits, open files, accounting and I/O information.
The set of values in the CPU registers, program counter and stack pointer that a process needs to resume exactly where it stopped.
New, Ready, Running, Waiting and Terminated: the five states a process moves through from creation (admitted) to completion (exit).
The kernel code that actually hands the CPU to the process the scheduler chose; it performs the context switch and enters user mode.
Saving the running process's CPU context into its PCB and loading another PCB's context into the CPU, so the CPU changes owner.
The time the dispatcher takes to stop one process and start another; it is pure overhead because no user code runs during it.
The job scheduler that picks which programs are admitted from the job pool into memory, controlling the degree of multiprogramming.
The scheduler that swaps a process out to disk (suspended state) to reduce memory pressure, and swaps it back later.
The CPU scheduler that picks the next process from the ready queue; it runs very often, so it must be fast.
The system call that creates a new child process as a copy of the parent; it returns 0 in the child and the child's pid in the parent.
The system call family that replaces a process's code and data with a new program, keeping the same pid.
Two or more processes attach the same region of memory and read and write it directly, with synchronization arranged by the processes themselves.
Processes exchange data by send and receive calls handled by the kernel, so no shared address space is needed and the kernel can enforce control.
A one-way byte stream between a writer and a reader process, usually connected through a shared file descriptor; a named pipe (FIFO) also exists as a file.
The unit of CPU use inside a process; threads share code, data and open files but each keeps its own program counter, registers and stack.
Many user threads are multiplexed onto a smaller or equal number of kernel threads, so blocking one thread does not block the others.
The OS may take the CPU away from a running process, on a timer interrupt or a higher-priority arrival, and give it to another ready process.
Preemptive scheduling in FCFS order with a fixed time quantum q; each process runs at most q and then goes to the tail of the ready queue.
In Linux CFS, the CPU time a task has received, weighted by its priority; the task with the smallest value runs next.

takeaways: A process is a program in execution, and the OS represents it by a PCB whose state field moves New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated.
The long-term scheduler admits jobs, the short-term scheduler picks the next ready process on every few milliseconds, and the medium-term scheduler swaps processes to disk.
A context switch is pure overhead: the dispatcher saves one CPU context and restores another, and dispatch latency is time no user process is running.
Processes are created by fork, reshaped by exec, ended by exit, and the parent collects the child's status and pid through wait.
Shared memory is fastest but needs the processes to synchronize themselves; message passing and pipes are slower but the kernel gives control and safety.
A thread is the unit of CPU use; threads of one process share code and data but each has its own program counter, registers and stack.
Scheduling criteria such as CPU utilization, throughput, waiting time and response time conflict, so choosing an algorithm is a trade-off.
FCFS suffers the convoy effect, SJF gives the minimum average waiting time but needs burst lengths and can starve long jobs, and priority scheduling starves unless aged.
Round robin is fair and good for time-sharing, and the time quantum decides whether it drifts towards FCFS (large q) or towards overhead (small q).
Linux moved from the O(1) scheduler's active and expired priority arrays to CFS, which orders tasks in a red-black tree by virtual runtime and gives CPU in proportion to weight.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a labelled state diagram or Gantt chart, the formulas for waiting and turnaround time, and a short comparison table, so draw the diagram and show every calculation step.

bank.q: Define a process. Draw the five-state process diagram and explain every transition, naming the events admitted, dispatch, I/O request, I/O done and exit. List the fields of the process control block and say why each is needed.
outline: Process = program in execution with code, data, stack, registers, program counter
States New, Ready, Running, Waiting, Terminated
admitted: New → Ready; dispatch: Ready → Running
I/O request: Running → Waiting; I/O done: Waiting → Ready
Running → Ready on preemption; exit: Running → Terminated
PCB fields: pid, state, program counter, CPU registers, memory limits, open files, accounting, I/O status
PCB lets the OS stop and restart a process without losing its place

bank.q: Explain the three process schedulers: long-term, short-term and medium-term. What does each control, how often does it run, and how does each affect system performance?
outline: Long-term: job pool → memory, controls degree of multiprogramming, runs rarely, should mix CPU-bound and I/O-bound jobs
Short-term: ready queue → CPU, runs every few milliseconds, must be very fast
Medium-term: swaps a process out (suspended) and back, reduces memory pressure
Too few admitted → idle CPU; too many → each gets little CPU and swapping increases
Cost of each in terms of overhead

bank.q: Explain the system calls fork(), exec(), wait() and exit() with a short program. How many processes does a program with two fork() calls create, and what does each fork() return?
outline: fork creates a child that is a copy of the parent; returns 0 in child, child pid in parent, -1 on failure
exec replaces the process image, same pid, no return on success
wait blocks the parent until a child ends and returns the child's pid and status
exit terminates the process and returns a status to the parent; orphans reparented to init/systemd
Two fork calls give 4 processes; count 2^n for n forks
Zombie: child exited but parent has not called wait

bank.q: Compare inter-process communication by shared memory, by message passing and by pipes. For each, state how data moves, whether the kernel is involved, what synchronization is needed and one typical use.
outline: Shared memory: one region mapped into both address spaces, kernel only sets it up, fastest, processes must synchronize, used for large data exchange
Message passing: send/receive calls, kernel copies each message, works across machines, kernel can control and order messages, direct or indirect (mailbox)
Pipes: one-way byte stream, unnamed (related processes, via file descriptor) and named/FIFO (unrelated processes, appears in file system)
Blocking vs non-blocking send and receive
Trade-off: speed versus control and safety

bank.q: Compare a process and a thread. Explain the many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many multithreading models, and list the benefits of multithreading.
outline: Thread: unit of CPU use; shares code, data, heap, open files; has own program counter, registers, stack
Process creation is heavier than thread creation; threads share, processes do not
Many-to-one: many user threads on one kernel thread — efficient, but one blocking call blocks all, no parallelism
One-to-one: each user thread has a kernel thread — true parallelism, but kernel thread count must be limited
Many-to-many: multiplex m user threads on ≤ m kernel threads — flexible, complex
Benefits: responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability on multicore

bank.q: Five processes arrive at time 0 with burst times 6, 8, 7, 3 and 4 ms. Draw the Gantt chart and compute average waiting time and average turnaround time for (a) FCFS and (b) non-preemptive SJF. Which is better and why?
outline: FCFS: run in arrival order; waiting time = start − arrival; turnaround = completion − arrival
Waitings: 0, 6, 14, 21, 24 → average 13 ms
SJF order 3, 4, 6, 7, 8: waitings 0, 3, 7, 13, 20 → average 8.6 ms
SJF gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set
SJF needs burst lengths in advance and can starve long jobs
Show every step of both Gantt charts

bank.q: For four processes with arrival times 0, 1, 2, 3 ms, priorities (smaller number = higher priority) 3, 1, 4, 2 and burst times 8, 4, 9, 5 ms, draw the Gantt chart for priority scheduling (a) non-preemptive and (b) preemptive. Compute average waiting time in both cases.
outline: Non-preemptive: highest-priority process runs to completion once started
Preemptive: a newly arrived higher-priority process takes the CPU at once
Table of start, completion, waiting and turnaround times
Compare both averages
Starvation of low priority; fix with aging
Convention that smaller number = higher priority stated explicitly

bank.q: Four processes of burst times 5, 4, 3 and 2 ms arrive together. Run round robin with time quantum 2 ms and draw the Gantt chart. Compute average waiting time, then explain what happens if the quantum becomes very large and if it becomes very small.
outline: Ready queue in arrival order; each turn at most 2 ms; unfinished process joins the tail
Waiting time = completion − arrival − burst; average it
Large q → behaves like FCFS, poor response time
Small q → many context switches, dispatch latency dominates
Rule of thumb: q large relative to context switch time

bank.q: A process executes fork(). In the child, it calls exec() to run a new program, and the parent calls wait(). Trace the state changes of both PCBs from creation to termination, and say what wait() returns and why a zombie would appear if the parent skipped wait().
outline: Parent Running, calls fork → child PCB created in Ready
Parent may go to Waiting inside wait(); child becomes Running
exec keeps the same pid but replaces the address space; call returns only on error
Child calls exit → Terminated, status kept; parent moves Ready and reads status
Without wait, the terminated child's PCB stays as a zombie
Orphan children are reparented to init/systemd

bank.q: Explain the convoy effect in FCFS with an example. Then compare FCFS, SJF, priority scheduling and round robin on average waiting time, starvation and preemption, and recommend an algorithm for a time-sharing system and for a batch system.
outline: Convoy effect: one long CPU-bound job delays many short I/O-bound jobs; CPU and devices both idle
FCFS: simple, non-preemptive, poor response time, convoy effect, no starvation
SJF: minimum average waiting time, needs future knowledge, starves long jobs, non-preemptive or preemptive (SRTF)
Priority: flexible, preemptive or not, starvation unless aging is used
RR: preemptive, fair, good response, overhead depends on quantum
Recommend RR for time-sharing, SJF or priority with aging for batch

bank.q: Define the scheduling criteria: CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time and response time, with formulas. Explain why no single algorithm maximises all of them, using at least two examples.
outline: Utilization = busy time / total time; throughput = processes completed per unit time
Turnaround = completion − arrival; waiting = time spent in ready queue; response = first CPU − arrival
FCFS minimises overhead but hurts response time
SJF minimises average waiting time but needs burst lengths and hurts long jobs
Small quantum improves response time but raises context switch overhead and lowers throughput
Trade-off statements must name the two conflicting criteria

bank.q: How does thread scheduling differ from process scheduling when several CPUs are available and some tasks have deadlines? Discuss contention scope, processor affinity, load balancing, and the rate-monotonic and earliest-deadline-first algorithms.
outline: Process-contention scope: threads of one process compete; system-contention scope: all threads compete
User threads scheduled onto lightweight threads, then to CPUs
Asymmetric vs symmetric multiprocessing; symmetric is standard
Processor affinity: soft and hard, to keep cache contents
Load balancing by push and pull migration, which fights affinity
Rate monotonic: fixed priority, shorter period → higher priority
EDF: dynamic priority, nearest deadline first; admits a task set only if utilization ≤ 1

bank.q: Compare the Linux O(1) scheduler and the Completely Fair Scheduler. Explain the active and expired arrays, the CFS red-black tree and virtual runtime, and judge which design handles a mix of interactive and batch tasks better.
outline: O(1): 140 priority levels, each with an active and an expired array, so picking the next task is constant time
Task runs and then moves to the expired array; arrays swap when active is empty; interactivity heuristics boost sleepers
Heuristics were hard to tune for the desktop, causing fairness complaints
CFS: red-black tree keyed on virtual runtime, leftmost node runs next
Virtual runtime grows in proportion to real runtime scaled by weight (nice value); smallest value chosen
No fixed time slice; target latency divided among runnable tasks
CFS is fairer and more predictable for mixed workloads but has more per-task bookkeeping

glossary.def: A program in execution, including its code, data, stack, program counter and current register values.
The CPU register that holds the address of the next instruction to execute for a process or thread.
The kernel data structure that stores everything the OS needs to know about one process, including its state and saved registers.
The set of processes in the Ready state, waiting for the CPU; it is normally a linked list of PCBs.
The number of processes currently in memory, controlled by the long-term scheduler.
The act of saving the running process's register state and loading another process's state so the CPU changes owner.
The kernel routine that performs the context switch, switches to user mode and jumps to the chosen process's next instruction.
The time between stopping one process and starting another; it is overhead.
The time from a process's arrival to its completion, equal to waiting time plus CPU time plus I/O time.
The total time a process spends in the ready queue waiting for the CPU.
The time from a request's arrival to the first response, measured from arrival to first CPU allocation in scheduling problems.
The number of processes completed per unit time.
The stretch of time a process runs on the CPU between two I/O requests.
Scheduling in which a process keeps the CPU until it blocks or terminates.
A situation in which a ready process waits indefinitely because other processes always have higher priority.
Gradually raising the priority of a waiting process so that it eventually runs.
The maximum time a process may run in one turn under round-robin scheduling, typically a few milliseconds.
The delay of many short processes behind one long CPU-bound process, as happens in FCFS.
A process that has terminated but whose PCB remains because the parent has not yet called wait.
A process whose parent has terminated, so it is adopted by init or systemd.
A thread that the OS itself schedules on the CPU, as opposed to a user thread managed by a library.
Keeping a thread on the processor it last ran on, to preserve cache contents.
The weighted amount of CPU time a task has received, used by CFS to choose the least-served task.
The set of all programs on disk that are waiting to be admitted into memory.
